newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN observers say Rwanda repatriation on track.
newsitem.headline: UN observers say Rwanda repatriation on track.

text.p: Some 500,000 Rwandans have gone home to their country from eastern Zaire and the situation of returnees is generally satisfactory, U.N. human rights observers reported on Tuesday.

Most returnees have arrived back in their native villages and communes, where local authorities are asking that soldiers of the former government army announce themselves and be registered, according to U.N. spokeswoman Therese Gastaut.

So far 500 ex-soldiers have been registered, according to the spokeswoman. She was reporting on information sent by the 110 U.N. human rights observers deployed in Rwanda to the U.N. High Commissioner for Human Rights, Jose Ayala-Lasso.
"In general, the situation of returnees continues to be generally satisfactory," Gastaut told a news briefing in Geneva.
Twenty-one people had been arrested as of November 23, according to the spokeswoman.

But in most cases they appear to have been detained for their own security, for example to avoid attacks by genocide survivors who suspect them of involvement in killings, according to the U.N. rights observers.

"The U.N. Human Rights Field Operation in Rwanda has been encouraged by the large number of reconciliation and re-integration meetings being held at the commune level. These involve local officials engaging in a dialogue with large numbers of residents on the importance of reconciliation and justice," the U.N. spokeswoman added.

The Rwandan government was continuing to disseminate information on the 15-day rule -- that people must move out of property within 15 days of it being claimed by its returning owner, according to the U.N. observers.

Ayala-Lasso, the top human rights official at the world body, has called for increasing the number of observers in Rwanda to 150 from 110 by year-end. He is also seeking $29 million to finance a total of 300 observers during 1997.
